decks.domain: Basic driving: starting, moving, stopping, steering methods and backing up

cards.front: Where should you look to learn how to start the vehicle you are driving?
cards.back: Because vehicles differ, look in your owner's manual to learn how to start the one you are driving.

cards.front: What are the steps for starting the engine?
cards.back: To start the engine, put your right foot on the brake pedal, confirm the gear selector is in park, then turn the key to the on position or push and release the start button.

cards.front: Which gear positions are used for starting the engine and for pulling away?
cards.back: The gear selector should be in park when you start the engine, and you move it to D for drive only when you are ready to pull away.
cards.memory_hook: Park to start, drive to go

cards.front: What should you check right after the engine starts?
cards.back: Once the engine runs, look over the gauges and any dashboard indicator lights that need attention, such as fuel, oil, ABS or air bag warnings.

cards.front: What do you do with the gear selector to pull away, and what do you check?
cards.back: To pull away, move the gear selector to D for drive and make sure the path ahead of the vehicle is safe.

cards.front: What else must you check before moving off?
cards.back: Before moving, also check the sides, the rear and your blind spots, looking over your shoulder for any traffic or obstacles.

cards.front: What comes just before you press the accelerator to pull away?
cards.back: Give a signal and, if it is safe, move your foot to the accelerator and press it gently.

cards.front: How should you build speed when pulling away?
cards.back: Build speed slowly and evenly, pressing the pedal with the top of your foot while your heel rests on the floor.

cards.front: What is the first step when you need to stop?
cards.back: To stop, first check your mirrors for traffic behind you, then shift your foot from the accelerator to the brake pedal.

cards.front: In what order do the mirror check and braking happen when stopping?
cards.back: Stopping begins with a mirror check for traffic behind you, and only then does your foot move from the accelerator to the brake.

cards.front: How should you press the brake until the vehicle stops?
cards.back: Keep steady pressure on the brake pedal until the vehicle has stopped.

decks.domain: Basic driving: starting, moving, stopping, steering methods and backing up

cards.front: Which way do you turn the wheel, forward or in reverse?
cards.back: You turn the steering wheel toward the direction you want the vehicle to go, whether you are moving forward or in reverse.

cards.front: How should you hold the steering wheel?
cards.back: Hold the outside of the steering wheel with both hands on opposite sides, using a grip that is firm but gentle.

cards.front: How should your fingers and thumbs grip the wheel?
cards.back: Grip the wheel with your fingers rather than your palms, keep your thumbs up along its face, and never turn it while holding the inside of the rim.

cards.front: Where do your hands go on the wheel, picturing it as a clock?
cards.back: Picturing the wheel as a clock face, your left hand belongs in the seven to nine o'clock area and your right hand in the three to five o'clock area.
cards.memory_hook: Seven to nine, three to five

cards.front: When may one hand leave the steering wheel?
cards.back: Both hands stay on the wheel at all times except when one is needed for another driving task, such as shifting gears, switching on the wipers or giving hand signals.

cards.front: Which hand signals may take one hand off the wheel?
cards.back: The hand signals that may take one hand off the wheel are those for turning, slowing or stopping.

cards.front: Where should a beginner first practice handling a vehicle?
cards.back: When you first learn to handle a car or truck, pick lightly traveled rural roads if you can.

cards.front: When are you ready to practice turning and parking?
cards.back: When you can steer accurately and keep making the small corrections steering always needs, you are ready to practice skills such as turning and parking.

cards.front: Why are lower hand positions on the wheel recommended?
cards.back: Keeping the hands in the seven to nine and three to five o'clock areas tends to reduce muscle strain, which means less steering that causes weaving within a lane.

decks.domain: Basic driving: starting, moving, stopping, steering methods and backing up

cards.front: When is hand-over-hand steering used?
cards.back: Hand-over-hand steering is for turning the wheel at low speeds, for example at an intersection or while parking.

cards.front: Where do your hands start for hand-over-hand steering?
cards.back: For hand-over-hand steering, start with your left hand between eight and nine o'clock and your right hand between three and four o'clock.

cards.front: Which part of the wheel do you use to turn right or left in hand-over-hand steering?
cards.back: In hand-over-hand steering you use the right top third of the wheel to turn right and the left top third to turn left, repeating as needed, then reverse the process to straighten out.

cards.front: When is one-hand steering allowed?
cards.back: One-hand steering is only for backing up or for a short reach to controls such as the wipers, flashers or lights.

cards.front: Where does your other hand stay while you reach for a control?
cards.back: When you must reach for a control, keep your other hand at the normal operating position of eight to nine or three to four o'clock, depending on how the wheel is designed.

cards.front: Which hand position does the hand that stays on the wheel keep during a reach?
cards.back: While one hand reaches for a control, the hand that stays on the wheel keeps the normal operating position of eight to nine or three to four o'clock, the same areas where hand-over-hand steering starts.

cards.front: Why must one hand stay on the wheel at all times?
cards.back: Keeping one hand on the wheel at all times matters for vehicle balance, for handling steering reversals and for avoiding injury.

decks.domain: Basic driving: starting, moving, stopping, steering methods and backing up

cards.front: When is a twelve o'clock hand position recommended?
cards.back: A twelve o'clock hand position is recommended only when you back up to the left or right and must turn in your seat to see the path behind you.

cards.front: In which situation does the manual recommend the twelve o'clock position?
cards.back: Backing up is the only situation in which the manual recommends the twelve o'clock position, and its backing steps put the left hand there.

cards.front: What should you do before getting in to back up?
cards.back: Check behind the vehicle before you get in, because children and small objects cannot be seen from the driver's seat.

cards.front: What are the first steps for backing up?
cards.back: To back up, keep your foot on the brake, shift into reverse and take hold of the wheel at twelve o'clock with your left hand.

cards.front: Where should you look while backing up?
cards.back: Rest your right arm on the back of the passenger seat and look straight out through the rear window.

cards.front: What do mirrors miss while you are backing?
cards.back: Glance at your mirrors from time to time while backing, knowing they do not show the area right behind the vehicle, and check a rearview camera now and then if you have one.

cards.front: While reversing, what is your main view and what is only an occasional check?
cards.back: When reversing, your main view comes from turning to look through the rear window, while mirrors and a camera are only checked now and then.

cards.front: How fast should you go in reverse, and why?
cards.back: Accelerate gently and keep your speed low in reverse, because a vehicle is much harder to steer when backing.

cards.front: Which way should you steer while backing?
cards.back: While backing, steer a little toward the side you want the rear of the vehicle to move.

cards.front: What checks do you make if you turn while backing up?
cards.back: If you are turning while you back up, make quick checks to the front and both sides.

cards.front: How long should you keep looking back while reversing?
cards.back: Keep looking toward the rear until the vehicle comes to a complete stop.

cards.front: What two things stay constant while backing up?
cards.back: When backing you steer slightly toward where the rear should go, and your rearward look continues until the vehicle has fully stopped.

recap_hooks.text: Start with your foot on the brake and the gear in park, check the gauges, then shift to drive, check all around, signal and accelerate gently.
To stop, check your mirrors first, then brake with steady pressure.
Grip the outside of the wheel with your fingers, hands low on the clock face, and keep both hands on the wheel except for driving tasks.
Hand-over-hand is for slow turns, and one-hand steering is only for backing or a quick reach to a control.
Check behind before getting in, hold the wheel at twelve o'clock with your left hand, look through the rear window and back up slowly.

merges.justification: The accepted wordings of sec06-F17, F19, F20 and F22 write push-pull with a slash, which fails the spoken-form lint, so when push-pull is used, how it works, how to reverse it and its crash benefit are taught on the lower-hands card's teaching, in the lesson and in their own exam items.

The accepted wording of sec06-F18 writes push-pull with a slash, which fails the spoken-form lint, so the push-pull starting positions are taught on the basic hand-position card's teaching, in the lesson and in their own exam item.

The accepted wording of sec06-R04 writes push-pull with a slash, which fails the spoken-form lint, so arms staying next to the body is taught on the both-hands card's teaching, in the lesson and in its own exam item.

The accepted wordings of sec06-F23 and sec06-R05 write push-pull with a slash, which fails the spoken-form lint, so push-pull being preferred, the two and ten warning and the method contrast are taught on the hand-over-hand card's teaching, in the lesson and in their own exam items.
